land.text: the Yamato realm that the Asuka period takes over: Cliopatria's Asuka Japan outline, from Kyushu to Fukushima

successors.note: Kofun period page: 'The introduction of Buddhism in 538 marked the transition from the Kofun to the Asuka period.' Cliopatria's Asuka row starts in 540, the asuka-japan dossier in 538.

capitals.name: Makimuku (Nara Basin)
capitals.note: Yamato polity page: Makimuku (Garenguma) is regarded as 'the birthplace of the Yamato court' and the early tombs lie in the south-eastern Nara Basin. The Kofun period page says the court had 'no permanent capital'; the coordinates are the researcher's placement at Sakurai.

capitals.name: Kawachi Plain (Osaka area)
capitals.note: Yamato polity page: 'the center moved there in the first half of the 5th century' (Kondayama, Daisen tombs); the year is the middle of that half-century. The page gives no seat for the 6th century; Keitai 'took about 20 years to enter the Nara Basin'. Coordinates are the researcher's placement near the Furuichi and Mozu tomb groups.

correction.text: the Yamato Kingship's core, 'Yamato Province' (Nara Prefecture) around Makimuku and Mount Miwa

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria has no Yamato before 540. The Kofun period page: the Yamato Kingship 'is usually believed to have begun c. 250' and its rulers held 'hegemony in Yamato until the 4th century'. The Yamato polity page says researchers date the establishment from the mid-3rd to the early 4th century. About 4,300 km2 by the gazetteer; no page gives an area. The extent is the researcher's reading of 'Yamato' (confidence 2).

correction.text: the Nara Basin and the Kawachi Plain, where the centre moved in the first half of the 5th century; the allied western lands are a vassal tint in the ledger

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: keyhole tombs spread 'from Yamato to Kawachi' and 'throughout the country during the 5th century' (Kofun period page), the centre moves to the Kawachi Plain (Yamato polity page), but Kibi, northern Kanto, Hyuga and Tsukushi keep their own leaders until the miyake of the 6th century. The direct land is the Kinki; Chugoku, Fukuoka and, from 450, the rest of the later Asuka outline are the ledger's vassal tint. The Kinki is a coarse stand-in (about 39,000 km2 by the gazetteer) for a court that held its core directly.

correction.text: the Yamato realm of the Keitai and Kinmei era: Cliopatria's Asuka Japan outline, the lands under the court's direct-control miyake after the Iwai Rebellion

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: from 528 (the end of the Iwai Rebellion, which 'ended' Tsukushi's autonomy with the founding of Daizaifu) to 538 the realm is the Asuka outline Cliopatria draws from 540: Kyushu to Fukushima (about 241,500 km2). The Yamato polity page says direct-control miyake were 'established across regions, especially after the Iwai Rebellion (527)' and the Kofun period page that 'During the 6th century, the Yamato clans began to dominate the southern half of Japan'. The extent of the Asuka outline in the north (Kanto to Fukushima) rests on the tomb horizon, not on a page that names a border.

region.text: Yamato, the Nara Basin around Makimuku

ledger.note: c. 250: the Yamato Kingship begins in the Nara Basin. 'The Yamato Kingship is usually believed to have begun c. 250'; the Yamato polity page gives mid-3rd to early 4th century depending on the researcher, with burial-mound evidence pointing to the later 3rd century.

region.text: western Honshu, where 'By 350, Yamato rule extended to western Honshu and northern Kyushu'

ledger.note: By 350: the west under Yamato. The Iwai Rebellion page: 'By 350, Yamato rule extended to western Honshu and northern Kyushu'; the Yamato polity page calls Kibi 'an important ally of the Yamato', one of the chiefs of the coalition and a regional state 'of considerable scale' with its own large keyhole tombs in the first half of the 5th century, so the tint, not the core, is drawn. [note corrected by reviewer jk-01-x, 2026-10-19: the page does not call Kibi a rival]
By 350: northern Kyushu under Yamato. The same sentence of the Iwai Rebellion page; Tsukushi kept its own governor and 'semi-autonomy' until 528.

region.text: the Kawachi Plain and the rest of the Kinki, where 'the center moved there in the first half of the 5th century'

ledger.note: Mid-5th century: the court's centre moves to the Kawachi Plain (Kondayama, Daisen tombs). The page gives 'the first half of the 5th century', not a year: 425 is the researcher's midpoint (confidence 1). The Kofun period page: keyhole tombs spread 'from Yamato to Kawachi'.

region.text: the rest of the later Asuka outline: Shikoku, Chubu, Kanto, southern Kyushu and southern Tohoku, where regional leaders of Kibi-like standing (Kanto, Hyuga, the Sendai plain) joined the Yamato tomb horizon

ledger.counterpart: Regional leaders of the east and south
ledger.note: 5th century: the tomb horizon reaches the whole later Asuka outline. 'Keyhole tombs spread from Yamato to Kawachi and then throughout the country during the 5th century' (Kofun period page); the Yamato polity page lists Kantō, Hyūga and the Sendai plain among the important regional leaders. Year is the researcher's midpoint; a court-to-chief relation is inferred from the tombs, no page names tribute (confidence 1).

527: Iwai rises in Tsukushi. The rebellion 'took place in Tsukushi Province, Japan' in 527 AD, in what is now Ogōri, Fukuoka Prefecture; Iwai, its governor, allied with Silla to block Yamato aid to Korea.
528: Iwai is crushed. 'Iwai was overthrown and executed'; infobox 'Yamato victory', 527-528. Mononobe no Arakabi led the Yamato army.
528: Tsukushi's autonomy ends. 'his area's autonomy ended with the founding of Daizaifu Fortress'; power in northern Kyushu later passed to the Ōtomo.

region.text: Tsukushi Province, brought under the court's direct rule

ledger.note: 528: northern Kyushu passes to direct rule (Daizaifu). The page says the autonomy ended; 'direct rule' is the researcher's reading of the founding of the fortress.

After 527: the western lands under direct control. 'After Keitai, direct-control miyake were established across regions, especially after the Iwai Rebellion (527)'; no page dates the end of Kibi's standing. The year bridges to Cliopatria's Asuka outline (confidence 1).

region.text: the rest of the later Asuka outline: Shikoku, Chubu, Kanto, southern Kyushu and southern Tohoku, where regional leaders of Kibi-like standing (Kanto, Hyuga, the Sendai plain) joined the Yamato tomb horizon

ledger.counterpart: Regional leaders of the east and south
ledger.note: After 527: the east and south under the miyake. Same sentence as above; the researcher bridges to the Asuka outline that starts in 540 (confidence 1).

region.text: the rest of the Asuka outline: western Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu, Chubu, Kanto and southern Tohoku, now under direct-control miyake

ledger.note: 528: the realm reaches the Asuka outline. The Yamato polity page: miyake 'across regions, especially after the Iwai Rebellion (527)'; the Kofun period page: 'During the 6th century, the Yamato clans began to dominate the southern half of Japan'. Bridging judgment (confidence 1).

region.text: the Yamato realm, now the Asuka period's state

ledger.note: 538: the Kofun period ends. 'The introduction of Buddhism in 538 marked the transition from the Kofun to the Asuka period'; the asuka-japan dossier takes the same court and land from 538.

wars.name: Yamato campaigns in Korea
wars.outcome: No land change recorded in the archipelago: Japanese troops allied with Baekje invaded Korea and fought Silla and Goguryeo; the page records no Yamato holding there.
wars.note: Iwai Rebellion page: '391 and 404: Japanese troops, allied with Paekje, invaded Korea'. The Kofun period page says 'Mimana Nihon-fu' should not be used, and no Yamato territory in Korea is drawn.

wars.name: Iwai Rebellion
wars.outcome: Yamato victory: Iwai was overthrown and executed in 528 and the Daizaifu fortress ended Tsukushi's autonomy.

certainty.note: Every frontier is approximate: the pages give provinces, tomb horizons and a rebellion, no boundary.

sources.title: Yamato polity
sources.note: Origins mid-3rd to early 4th century; core in the Nara Basin (Makimuku); tomb spread from southern Tohoku to southern Kyushu; Kawachi Plain centre in the first half of the 5th century; Five Kings of Wa 438-478; Keitai and the Iwai Rebellion 527; miyake; Gaya lost by 562.

sources.title: Kofun period
sources.note: Infobox c. 3rd century-538; Yamato Kingship 'usually believed to have begun c. 250'; keyhole tombs from Yamato to Kawachi, 'throughout the country during the 5th century'; no permanent capital; 538 Buddhism marks the move to Asuka.

sources.title: Iwai Rebellion
sources.note: 527-528 rebellion in Tsukushi, northern Kyushu, Yamato victory; 'By 350, Yamato rule extended to western Honshu and northern Kyushu'; 391 and 404 Korea; Daizaifu 528.

notes: Written by jk-01-x on 2026-10-19 from three pages (Yamato polity, Kofun period, Iwai Rebellion). Cliopatria has no Yamato before 540; this dossier covers c. 250 to 538 and hands over to asuka-japan, whose predecessor slug is 'yamato'. Start: the Kofun period page says 'usually believed to have begun c. 250'; the Yamato polity page dates the establishment from the mid-3rd to the early 4th century and the Iwai page says 'late 3rd or early 4th'. The extent is thin: direct land = Nara to c. 425, the Kinki after; the Chugoku and northern Kyushu lands are a vassal tint from 'By 350' (Iwai page), the rest of the Asuka outline a tint from the 5th century (confidence 1, from the tomb horizon), all folded into direct land in 528 (confidence 1). Events at confidence 1: 425, 450, and the 528 east/south and western Honshu steps. Not on the pages: Himiko and Yamatai (the Yamato polity page puts Himiko in Yamatai in the first half of the 3rd century and a merger with Kunu-no-kuni; no extent), Mimana/Gaya territory (not drawn), Hayato and Emishi (the Kofun page does not mention them; the emishi dossier has the north), Kibi's fall (undated). Rulers: the Five Kings of Wa have titles (Chin 438, Sei 443 and 451, Kō 462, Bu 478) but no reign years on the pages, so no ruler strip. Area comparison not applicable (no infobox area). Counterpart strings 'Kibi and western Honshu', 'Tsukushi (northern Kyushu)' and 'Regional leaders of the east and south' are vassals named as the pages give them; no dossier is planned.
